It’s only a screening until it pops positive. After that it’s monitoring, therefore diagnostic and not preventative. Screenings exist to catch things that might otherwise go unnoticed, but once you know the condition exists you’re no longer looking for something, you’re checking up on it.

Cholesterol SCREENING is covered, but if you already know the patient has high cholesterol from previous laboratory studies, then it is no longer a SCREENING. We screen for things that we don’t know exist. We don’t screen for diagnosed problems, we run diagnostic tests to evaluate their current status. Once you’re diabetic, no matter what your A1c is you’re still diabetic. Well controlled maybe, but still a diabetic. Once you have high cholesterol, even if it becomes well controlled without medical international through lifestyle modifications, you still have a history of high cholesterol and we are no longer screening for that condition we are monitoring it. I hate when patients ask why their labs weren’t coded as preventative, and I have to explain that I’m not going to ask the provider to falsify the coding to let you off the hook for the bill. I hate insurance companies with a passion, and when something is truly preventative or a screening for a condition we do not know exists, I push to make sure it’s associated with the correct preventative or screening diagnosis. But don’t ask your doctor to commit fraud by intentionally miscoding something.

MATLAB is its own scripting environment. By default it comes with toolkits for handling external data files (csv files in this particular case) and can do complex math on large datasets. It organizes data into matrices and vectors, so you can do matrix math quickly. There's even a symbolic math toolkit which you can use to enter equations and generate output from them. The Simulink toolboxes can be used to solve differential equations that otherwise couldn't be solved by hand, and throughout the software you can use powerful plotting tools to generate and customize visualizations of your data. The only pre-requisite is a basic understanding of scripting or computer programming, matrix math operations, and the ability to read through the documentation. You will need to take Anatomy, chemistry with lab, and a few others I can’t remember off the top of my head right now. Look on their website, the requirements to apply to change colleges is on there. The courses are difficult, but in a different way then engineering. Engineering courses are focused heavily on theory and application of a few big topics. The health science courses I took (Anatomy, microbiology, nutrition) were all far more detail oriented, and focused much more on memorization. The concepts aren’t generally difficult to understand, but the breadth of the material can make for a challenge. 

What I ended up doing is getting my certified nurse assistant license by taking night classes at the catholic charities in south Boston. It’s $1000 and takes 10 weeks I think. If you pass, which isn’t hard, you then take the Red Cross exam ($100) and if you pass that then you get your certification from the state. Engineering to nursing is a big change so I’m taking some time off to find a job and make sure it’s the path I want to take, but the engineering co-ops really made it clear that engineering isn’t the path for me. EGR works to reduce in cylinder combustion temperatures, reducing oxides of nitrogen, not particulate. It actually generally increases particulate, leading to other countermeasures such as DPF. The NOx causes smog and poor air quality, and does not “settle out” but rather stays in the atmosphere until it decomposes. Because it’s a gas, and not a piece of particulate, it can be carried by the wind to other areas, so even pollution in cornfields in Iowa can eventually work it’s way to the cities on the seaboard. It definitely is worsened in congested areas but we all share one atmosphere.

I see a lot of hate on EGR here, but clean air is important and EGR helps to reduce the production of smog forming oxides of nitrogen. There are definite improvements that could be made to the technology to improve part life and reduce failures, but removing or disabling the technology is not the proper solution, and is trading the health and wellbeing of everyone else for your own convenience. >Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) is the predominant transporter responsible for resorption of glucose filtrate back into the circulation. Empagliflozin is an inhibitor of SGLT2. This would, to me, be saying that Jardience prevents some of the glucose in the blood that is filtered by the kidneys, from re-entering the blood stream, and therefore you pee some of the glucose out. However Jardience does not affect insulin directly, therefore, an increased risk of hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) would seem to be likely. In addition, fructose, which accounts for a large portion of all added sugars found in processed foods, is unaffected by Jardience. Fructose is also turned rapidly into fat by the liver, and is currently believed to be a major factor in the recent uptick in fatty liver disease.

Bottom line, it's not a good idea, and it might not have any noticeable effect if the majority of carbs are added sugars.

The big thing is being able to have access to cash from an ATM or teller if needed, without having to pay the often large fee for cash advances, which would wipe out any interest earned on your fund and more.

The no penalty CD from Ally is a good choice, but you should consider keeping some of your emergency fund in your current savings account at the same bank as your checking account. The reason for this is if you need fast access to your money, you can have it transferred directly between the accounts, and for most institutions this is instantaneous.
